Trapezius.action: Elevates, depresses and retracts scapula; rotates glenoid cavity superiorly
Trapezius.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 41

Levator scapulae.action: Elevates scapula; rotates to depress glenoid cavity

Rhomboids (major and minor).action: Retract scapula; rotate to depress glenoid cavity; fix scapula to thoracic wall

Rhomboids (major and minor).src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 43

Latissimus dorsi.action: Extends, adducts and medially rotates humerus
Latissimus dorsi.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 42

Serratus posterior superior.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 40

Serratus posterior inferior.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 40

Erector spinae (Spinalis (medial), longi.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 46

Splenius.action: Bilaterally: extend head and neck; unilaterally: laterally flex and rotate head and neck

Splenius.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 47

Transversospinalis.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 48

Pectoralis major.action: Adducts, flexes and medially rotates humerus

Pectoralis minor.action: Stabilizes scapula by drawing it inferiorly and anteriorly against thoracic wall

clinical: Long thoracic nerve lesion: winged scapula, medial border lifts off thoracic wall when pushing with the upper limb

Deltoid.action: Anterior head: flexes and medially rotates arm; middle head: abducts arm; posterior head: extends and laterally rotates arm
clinical: Myotome: C5 and C6

Supraspinatus.action: First 15 degrees of arm abduction; stabilizes glenohumeral joint
clinical: Rotator cuff muscle; supraspinous fossa to greater tubercle, beneath subdeltoid/subacromial bursa

Infraspinatus.action: Lateral rotation of arm; stabilizes glenohumeral joint
clinical: Rotator cuff muscle; infraspinous fossa to greater tubercle
Has its own strength test in rotator cuff disease examination

Teres minor.action: Lateral rotation of arm; stabilizes glenohumeral joint
clinical: Rotator cuff muscle; lateral border of scapula to greater tubercle

Subscapularis.action: Medially rotates arm; stabilizes glenohumeral joint
clinical: Rotator cuff muscle; subscapular fossa to lesser tubercle
Has its own strength test in rotator cuff disease examination

Biceps brachii.action: Strong supinator; flexes forearm; weak shoulder flexor; resists dislocation
clinical: Proximal biceps tendinopathy: anterior shoulder pain, tender in intertubercular groove, worse with shoulder/elbow flexion when supinated

Bicipital reflex tests integrity of C5 and C6

Coracobrachialis.action: Flexes arm; adducts arm; resists dislocation

Triceps.action: Together extend elbow; long head extends shoulder joint and resists shoulder dislocation

Palmaris longus.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 8

Pronator teres.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 6

Flexor carpi radialis.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 7

Flexor carpi ulnaris.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 9

Flexor digitorum superficialis.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 10

Flexor digitorum profundus.action: Flexes wrist; flexes IP joints in digits 2-5
Flexor digitorum profundus.innervation: Lateral part (digits 2 & 3): median nerve; medial part (digits 4 & 5): ulnar nerve
clinical: Its medial part is the 'half' muscle of the 1½ anterior compartment muscles supplied by the ulnar nerve.
Flexor digitorum profundus.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 12

Flexor pollicis longus.action: Flexes wrist; flexes MCP & IP joint of digit 1
Flexor pollicis longus.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 13

Pronator quadratus.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 14

Brachioradialis.action: Weakly flexes the forearm; strongest in mid-pronated position ("drinking muscle")
clinical: Forms the lateral border of the cubital fossa.
Brachioradialis.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 19

Extensor carpi radialis longus.action: Extends and abducts wrist; active during fist clenching
Extensor carpi radialis longus.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 20

clinical: Lateral epicondylosis (tennis elbow) is predominantly a tendinopathy of extensor carpi radialis brevis.
Extensor carpi radialis brevis.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 20

Extensor digitorum.action: Extends MCP joints primarily, IP joints secondarily (digits 2-5); also extends wrist
Extensor digitorum.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 21

Extensor digiti minimi.action: Extends digit 5 (MCP joint primarily, IP joints secondarily); also extends wrist
Extensor digiti minimi.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 21

Extensor carpi ulnaris.action: Extends and adducts wrist; active during fist clenching
Extensor carpi ulnaris.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 22

Supinator.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 24

Extensor indicis.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 25

Abductor pollicis longus.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 26

clinical: Its tendon outlines the anatomical snuff box (radial artery over scaphoid and trapezium).
Extensor pollicis brevis.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 26

clinical: Its tendon outlines the anatomical snuff box (radial artery over scaphoid and trapezium).
Extensor pollicis longus.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 26

clinical: Carpal tunnel syndrome may cause thumb weakness (APB, abductor pollicis brevis).

Lumbricals.action: Flex the MCP joint; extend the IP joints
Lumbricals.innervation: Medial two: ulnar nerve; lateral two: median nerve

clinical: Ulnar canal (Guyon's canal) compression weakens the intrinsic hand muscles.

Gluteus maximus.action: Extension of hip; assists in standing from seated position
clinical: Myotome: S1.
Gluteus maximus.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 7

Gluteus medius/minimus.action: Abduction & medial rotation of thigh; gait stabilization
Gluteus medius/minimus.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 9

clinical: Myotome: L5.
Tensor fascia latae.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 8

Piriformis.action: Lateral rotation of thigh; abduction of thigh; stabilization of hip
clinical: Key gluteal landmark: superior gluteal vessels/nerve pass above it, inferior gluteal vessels/nerve and sciatic nerve below.
Piriformis syndrome is a listed cause of sciatic nerve injury.
Piriformis.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 11

Superior gemellus.action: Laterally rotate hip; stabilize head of femur in acetabulum
Superior gemellus.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 10

Obturator internus.action: Laterally rotate hip; stabilize head of femur in acetabulum
Obturator internus.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 10

Inferior gemellus.action: Laterally rotate hip; stabilize head of femur in acetabulum
Inferior gemellus.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 10

Quadratus femoris.action: Laterally rotate hip; stabilize head of femur in acetabulum
Quadratus femoris.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 10

clinical: Myotome: L1/2.
Iliopsoas.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 32

Sartorius.action: Lateral rotation of hip; flexion of hip; flexion of knee; hip abduction
clinical: Lateral boundary of the femoral triangle.
Part of pes anserinus (Sartorius, Gracilis, semiTendinosus: SGT).
Sartorius.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 33

Rectus femoris.action: Powerful knee extensor; flexes the hip
clinical: Patellar tendon reflex tests the integrity of L3-L4.
Myotome: L3/4.
Rectus femoris.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 34

clinical: Patellar tendon reflex tests the integrity of L3-L4.
Myotome: L3/4.
Vastus lateralis.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 34

clinical: Patellar tendon reflex tests the integrity of L3-L4.
Myotome: L3/4.
Vastus medialis.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 34

clinical: Patellar tendon reflex tests the integrity of L3-L4.
Myotome: L3/4.
Vastus intermedius.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 34

Biceps femoris.action: Extension of hip; flexion of knee
Biceps femoris.innervation: Long head: tibial division of sciatic nerve; short head: common peroneal division of sciatic nerve
clinical: Forms a boundary of the popliteal fossa.
Hamstrings myotome: L5.
Biceps femoris.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 22

Semitendinosus.action: Extension of hip; flexion of knee
clinical: Part of pes anserinus (SGT).
Forms a boundary of the popliteal fossa.
Semitendinosus.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 23

Semimembranosus.action: Extension of hip; flexion of knee
clinical: Forms a boundary of the popliteal fossa.
Semimembranosus.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 23

clinical: Medial boundary of the femoral triangle.
Groin pull: active contraction plus passive stretch of medial compartment; bruising, pain; RICE and NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs).
Adductor longus.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 40

clinical: Groin pull: active contraction plus passive stretch of medial compartment; treated conservatively.
Adductor brevis.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 40

Adductor magnus.action: Adductor part: adduction and flexion of hip; hamstring part: adduction and extension of hip
Adductor magnus.innervation: Adductor part: obturator nerve; hamstring part: tibial nerve
clinical: Adductor hiatus: femoral artery passes through to become the popliteal artery.
Adductor magnus.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 41

Gracilis.action: Adduction of hip; flexion of knee
clinical: Part of pes anserinus (SGT).
Gracilis.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 42

clinical: Myotome: L4 & L5
Supports the medial longitudinal and transverse arches; broad attachment on medial foot

Extensor digitorum longus.action: Dorsiflexes ankle; extends lateral four digits
clinical: Splits into 4 tendons on the dorsum of the foot; functions with extensor digitorum brevis
Myotome: L5

Fibularis longus.action: Everts foot; weakly plantarflexes ankle; supports transverse arch
clinical: Inserts on medial plantar foot; supports medial longitudinal and transverse arches

Fibularis brevis.action: Everts foot; weakly plantarflexes ankle; supports transverse arch
clinical: Inserts on base of 5th metatarsal

Gastrocnemius.action: Plantarflexes ankle with knee extended; flexes leg at knee
clinical: Myotome: S1
Inserts via calcaneal (Achilles) tendon: Achilles tendinopathy and rupture
Baker's cyst: synovial extension through the gastrocnemius/semimembranosus bursa into the popliteal fossa
Gastrocnemius strain or tendinopathy causes posterior knee pain
Myotome: S1
Inserts via calcaneal (Achilles) tendon: Achilles tendinopathy and rupture
Can be used for tendon grafts
Contracts to rotate the femur 5 degrees laterally, unlocking the screw-home mechanism so flexion can occur
Popliteus strain or tendinopathy causes posterior knee pain

Tibialis posterior.action: Plantarflexes ankle; inverts foot; supports longitudinal arches of foot
clinical: Myotome: L5
Most anterior structure in the tarsal tunnel (Tom, Dick, And Very Nervous Harry)
Tibialis posterior dysfunction: tendon hypovascular distal to medial malleolus; medial ankle pain, pes planus, 'too many toes' sign

Flexor digitorum longus.action: Flexes lateral four digits; plantarflexes ankle; supports longitudinal arches of foot
clinical: 'Dick' in the tarsal tunnel (Tom, Dick, And Very Nervous Harry), behind tibialis posterior

Flexor hallucis longus.action: Flexion of 1st digit; weakly plantarflexes ankle; supports medial longitudinal arch of foot
clinical: 'Harry', the most posterior tarsal tunnel structure; its tendon runs under the sustentaculum tali
Functions with extensor digitorum longus on the dorsum of the foot
Extensor digitorum brevis.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 4

clinical: Functions with extensor hallucis longus on the dorsum of the foot
Extensor hallucis brevis.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 4

Plantar fascia.action: Protects sole; supports longitudinal arches; holds everything together
clinical: Plantar fasciitis: pain at anteromedial calcaneus on first morning steps, worse with passive dorsiflexion, often with tight Achilles
Plantar fascia.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 5

vertebral.name: Vertebral artery
facts: Vertebral artery insufficiency is a vascular red flag in neck pain: dizziness with neck movement, cranial nerve abnormalities, drop attacks
src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 7

subclavian.name: Subclavian artery
facts: First segment of the upper extremity supply: subclavian, then axillary, then brachial artery
src: Neurovascular Supply to the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 3, 4, 9

axillary.name: Axillary artery
facts: Continues from the subclavian artery into the brachial artery, supplying the axilla
src: Neurovascular Supply to the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 3, 4, 9

brachial.name: Brachial artery
facts: Supplies the anterior compartment of the arm
Used to measure blood pressure (BP)
Susceptible to humeral shaft fractures
Supplies the anterior compartment, continuing as the radial and ulnar arteries.
In the cubital fossa with biceps tendon and median nerve (TAN: Tendon, Artery, Nerve).
Cubital fossa is pictured as the site for blood pressure measurement.
src: Neurovascular Supply to the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 5
Neurovascular Supply to the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 3, 6

deep_brachial.name: Profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery
facts: Branch of the brachial artery; arterial supply of the posterior compartment of the arm
src: Neurovascular Supply to the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 5, 6

radial.name: Radial artery
facts: Named after the brachial artery on the upper extremity blood supply overview
Radial pulse is taken at the wrist.
Supplies both anterior and posterior compartments of the forearm.
Crosses the anatomical snuff box over the scaphoid and trapezium.
Enters the hand laterally; contributes to the two palmar arterial arches, labelled leading into the deep palmar arch.
src: Neurovascular Supply to the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 3
Neurovascular Supply to the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 3, 4
Wrist and Hand, part 1, slide 67, 68

ulnar.name: Ulnar artery
facts: Named after the brachial artery on the upper extremity blood supply overview
Supplies the anterior compartment of the forearm, arising from the brachial artery.
Enters the hand medially, labelled leading into the superficial palmar arch.
Runs with the ulnar nerve within the ulnar (Guyon's) canal.
Lies superficial to the carpal tunnel.
src: Neurovascular Supply to the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 3
Neurovascular Supply to the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 3
Wrist and Hand, part 1, slide 67

sup_palmar_arch.name: Superficial palmar arch
facts: One of two palmar arterial arches; gives off the palmar digital arteries.
src: Wrist and Hand, part 1, slide 67, 68

deep_palmar_arch.name: Deep palmar arch
facts: Second palmar arterial arch, deep to the superficial arch, labelled continuous with the radial artery.
src: Wrist and Hand, part 1, slide 68

palmar_digital.name: Common and proper palmar digital arteries
facts: Palmar digital arteries arise from the superficial palmar arch to supply the digits.
src: Wrist and Hand, part 1, slide 67

sup_gluteal.name: Superior gluteal artery
facts: Exits the pelvis superior to piriformis, the key gluteal landmark.
src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 14

inf_gluteal.name: Inferior gluteal artery
facts: Exits inferior to piriformis.
Part of the collateral circulation around the hip.
src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 14, 48

obturator.name: Obturator artery
facts: Its branches, with perforating branches, supply the medial compartment of the thigh.
src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 55

external_iliac.name: External iliac artery
facts: Becomes the femoral artery deep to the inguinal ligament.
src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 47

femoral.name: Femoral artery
facts: Femoral pulse palpable below the inguinal ligament; in femoral triangle, order lateral to medial is NAVEL (nerve, artery, vein, empty canal, lymphatics).
Enclosed by the femoral sheath; passes the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal artery.
Its branches supply the anterior compartment of the thigh.
Shown continuing into the popliteal artery in the leg's arterial supply
src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 47, 49, 55
Anatomy of the Leg, slide 34, 35

deep_femoral.name: Deep femoral (profunda femoris) artery
facts: Branch of the femoral artery giving the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries and perforating branches.
Supplies the hip joint via the circumflex femoral arteries.
src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 47

perforating.name: Perforating arteries
facts: Perforating branches of the profunda femoris supply the posterior compartment of the thigh.
Part of the collateral circulation around the hip.
src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 26, 48

med_circumflex_femoral.name: Medial circumflex femoral artery
facts: Branch of the profunda femoris; supplies the hip joint and femoral head.
Part of the collateral circulation around the hip.
Displaced femoral neck fractures need surgery to preserve femoral head blood supply.
src: Clinical Approach to the Hip, slide 8, 27

lat_circumflex_femoral.name: Lateral circumflex femoral artery
facts: Branch of the profunda femoris; supplies the hip joint.
Part of the collateral circulation around the hip.
Its descending branch joins the collateral circulation around the knee.
src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 47, 48

popliteal.name: Popliteal artery
facts: Continuation of the femoral artery after the adductor hiatus.
Deepest content of the popliteal fossa (deep to superficial: artery, vein, nerve; AVN).
Knowledge check: painless pulsatile popliteal mass in an 85-year-old (diagnosis left blank on slide).
Divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries
Popliteal artery aneurysm is in the differential of a popliteal (Baker's) cyst
src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 27, 28, 47
Anatomy of the Leg, slide 34, 35

ligament_head_femur.name: Artery of the ligament of the head of the femur
facts: Carried in the ligament of the head of the femur; contributes to hip joint blood supply.
src: Clinical Approach to the Hip, slide 6, 8

ant_tibial.name: Anterior tibial artery
facts: Branch of the popliteal artery supplying the anterior leg
Continues onto the dorsal foot as the dorsalis pedis artery
src: Anatomy of the Leg, slide 34

post_tibial.name: Posterior tibial artery
facts: Branch of the popliteal artery; gives off the fibular artery
Runs in the tarsal tunnel ('A' in Tom, Dick, And Very Nervous Harry); divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries
Pulse felt between medial malleolus and calcaneal tendon; invert foot to relax flexor retinaculum; check both sides for symmetry
src: Anatomy of the Leg, slide 35

fibular.name: Fibular artery
facts: Branch of the posterior tibial artery in the posterior leg
src: Anatomy of the Leg, slide 35

dorsalis_pedis.name: Dorsalis pedis artery
facts: Continuation of the anterior tibial artery on the dorsal foot
Diminished or absent dorsalis pedis pulse usually indicates vascular insufficiency from arterial disease
Five P's of arterial occlusion: pain, pallor, paresthesia, paralysis, pulselessness
src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 38, 39

med_plantar.name: Medial plantar artery
facts: Branch of the posterior tibial artery supplying the plantar foot
src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 40

lat_plantar.name: Lateral plantar artery
facts: Branch of the posterior tibial artery supplying the plantar foot
src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 40

all.name: Anterior longitudinal ligament
facts: Vertebral ligament running along the front of the vertebral bodies
In whiplash, injured less often than muscles or facets (order: facets > anterior longitudinal ligament (ALL) > bones > cord)
src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 22, 54

pll.name: Posterior longitudinal ligament
facts: Vertebral ligament running along the back of the vertebral bodies
src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 22

supraspinous.name: Supraspinous ligament
facts: Vertebral ligament along the tips of the spinous processes
src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 22

interspinous.name: Interspinous ligament
facts: Vertebral ligament between adjacent spinous processes
src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 22

nuchal.name: Ligamentum nuchae
facts: Vertebral ligament of the neck, labelled on the vertebral ligaments slide
src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 22

acromioclavicular.name: Acromioclavicular ligament
facts: Stabilizes the acromioclavicular (AC) joint, a synovial plane joint
src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 11

coracoclavicular.name: Coracoclavicular ligament
facts: Joins coracoid process to clavicle at the acromioclavicular (AC) joint
src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 11

glenohumeral.name: Glenohumeral ligaments
facts: Three glenohumeral ligaments reinforce the joint capsule of the glenohumeral (GH) joint
Ligaments are an anatomic factor in shoulder stability; in instability they may be torn or stretched
src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 13, 14, 49, 50

coracoacromial.name: Coracoacromial ligament
facts: Spans coracoid process to acromion above the glenohumeral joint
src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 13, 50

coracohumeral.name: Coracohumeral ligament
facts: Labelled on the shoulder ligament anatomy figure with the glenohumeral and coracoacromial ligaments
src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 50

ucl.name: Ulnar (medial) collateral ligament
facts: Stabilizes the medial elbow.
Injured by chronic repetitive overuse (baseball pitchers); lax with no end point on valgus stress.
Reconstruction (Tommy John surgery) uses a tendon graft such as palmaris longus or semitendinosus.
src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 4, 23, 25

rcl_elbow.name: Radial (lateral) collateral ligament
facts: Lateral ligament of the elbow joint.
src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 4

annular_ligament.name: Anular ligament
facts: Holds the radial head at the proximal radioulnar joint and allows rotation.
Thinner and weaker distally in children, letting the radial head sublux (nursemaid's elbow).
src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 7, 22

interosseous_membrane_forearm.name: Interosseous membrane
facts: Connects radius and ulna (intermediate radioulnar syndesmosis).
Separates the anterior and posterior compartments of the forearm.
src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 5

flexor_retinaculum.name: Flexor retinaculum
facts: Median nerve passes deep to it; compression there is carpal tunnel syndrome.
Deep to the palmar carpal ligament; forms the roof of the carpal tunnel.
Carpal tunnel: floor carpal bones; contains median nerve and tendons of FPL (flexor pollicis longus), FDS, FDP.
src: Neurovascular Supply to the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 10
Wrist and Hand, part 2, slide 6, 11

extensor_retinaculum_wrist.name: Extensor retinaculum
facts: Six osseofibrous tunnels deep to it carry the extensor tendons in synovial sheaths.
src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 29

palmar_carpal.name: Palmar carpal ligament
facts: Labelled over the anterior compartment tendons at the wrist.
Thickening of the antebrachial fascia, continuous with the extensor retinaculum.
Superficial to the flexor retinaculum.
src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 4
Wrist and Hand, part 1, slide 50

sacrospinous.name: Sacrospinous ligament
facts: Named with the sacrotuberous ligament as boundaries of the greater and lesser sciatic foramina.
src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 4

sacrotuberous.name: Sacrotuberous ligament
facts: Named with the sacrospinous ligament as boundaries of the greater and lesser sciatic foramina.
src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 4

itb.name: Iliotibial (IT) band
facts: Insertion of tensor fascia latae and gluteus maximus; tensed by tensor fascia latae.

src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 7, 8
Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 2, slide 14

inguinal.name: Inguinal ligament
facts: Superior boundary of the femoral triangle (with sartorius and adductor longus).

src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 47, 49

ligament_head_femur.name: Ligament of the head of the femur
facts: Carries the artery of the ligament of the head of the femur.
src: Clinical Approach to the Hip, slide 6

acetabular_labrum.name: Acetabular labrum
facts: Hip joint associated structure, with hyaline cartilage and the articular capsule (balancing mobility and stability).

hip_capsular.name: Hip capsular ligaments (unnamed on slide)
facts: Colour-coded only: one ligament set limits extension, another (from the pubis) limits abduction.
src: Clinical Approach to the Hip, slide 7

acl.name: Anterior cruciate ligament
facts: Taut in extension; foot free, prevents tibia moving anteriorly under femur
Foot planted, prevents femur moving posteriorly on tibia
Not enclosed within the synovial membrane
src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 10, 12, 28

pcl.name: Posterior cruciate ligament
facts: Strongest cruciate; taut in flexion; foot planted, prevents femur moving anteriorly on tibia
Foot free, prevents tibia moving posteriorly under femur
Dashboard injury: torn when tibia is forced posteriorly relative to femur
src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 10, 12, 13

mcl.name: Tibial (medial) collateral ligament
facts: Medial meniscus is firmly adhered to it
Injured by valgus force, almost always in collisions; complete tear often with ACL (anterior cruciate ligament) tear
src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 8, 21, 26

lcl.name: Fibular (lateral) collateral ligament
facts: Injured by high-energy varus force; uncommon in isolation
Associated with PCL (posterior cruciate ligament) injuries; no swelling in isolation
src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 8, 22

medial_meniscus.name: Medial meniscus
facts: C-shaped, broader posteriorly, firmly adhered to tibial collateral ligament
Peripheral part richly vascularized; central part avascular, nourished by synovial fluid
Bucket-handle tear in the unhappy triad, since it is attached to the MCL (medial collateral ligament)
src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 26, 27, 39

lateral_meniscus.name: Lateral meniscus
facts: Nearly circular, smaller, freely movable; not as susceptible to injury
Menisci deepen and stabilize the joint and act as shock absorbers
src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 26

patellar_ligament.name: Patellar tendon
facts: Continuation of quadriceps femoris to the tibial tuberosity
May avulse from the tibial tuberosity in a PCL (posterior cruciate ligament) dashboard injury
src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 8, 13

atfl.name: Anterior talofibular ligament
facts: Lateral collateral ligament of the ankle; most often sprained (ATFL > CFL > PTFL)
Tested with the anterior drawer test
src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 17, 26, 27

calcaneofibular.name: Calcaneofibular ligament
facts: Lateral collateral ligament of the ankle; second most often sprained
src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 17, 26

ptfl.name: Posterior talofibular ligament
facts: Lateral collateral ligament of the ankle; least often sprained of the three
Dislocation happens when all three lateral ligaments are fully torn
src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 17, 26

deltoid_ankle.name: Deltoid ligament
facts: Medial collateral ligament of the ankle
Medial ankle sprain (catching foot on turf during kick); may rupture in a Maisonneuve fracture
src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 18, 26, 33

spring.name: Spring (calcaneonavicular) ligament
facts: Plantar foot ligament between calcaneus and navicular
src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 18, 20

long_plantar.name: Long plantar ligament
facts: Plantar foot ligament on the calcaneus
src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 20

interosseous_membrane_leg.name: Interosseous membrane
facts: Joins tibia and fibula, separating the leg compartments
src: Anatomy of the Leg, slide 5

flexor_retinaculum_ankle.name: Flexor retinaculum
facts: Deep posterior compartment tendons pass under it in the tarsal tunnel
Invert the foot to relax it when feeling the posterior tibial pulse
src: Anatomy of the Leg, slide 24

extensor_retinaculum_ankle.name: Extensor retinacula
facts: Labelled over the anterior compartment tendons at the ankle
src: Anatomy of the Leg, slide 10

plantar_fascia.name: Plantar fascia
facts: Protects sole; supports longitudinal arches; holds everything together
Plantar fasciitis: pain at anteromedial calcaneus on first morning steps, worse with passive dorsiflexion, often with tight Achilles
src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 5

spine.name: Vertebral column
facts: Protects spinal cord, supports body weight, aids posture and movement
Cervical and lumbar curves concave posteriorly (secondary); thoracic and sacral concave anteriorly (primary)
Abnormal curves: kyphosis, lordosis, scoliosis
spine.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 16, 17

spine.name: Vertebra (typical)
facts: Body, pedicles, laminae, transverse and spinous processes, articular processes; vertebral arch encloses vertebral foramen for spinal cord
Superior and inferior vertebral notches form the intervertebral foramen for the spinal nerve
spine.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 18

spine.name: Intervertebral disc
facts: Anulus fibrosus around nucleus pulposus; attaches vertebrae, permits movement, absorbs shock
Discogenic pain: axial-predominant, mechanical, aggravated by forward flexion
spine.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 19, 30

spine.name: Zygapophysial (facet) joints
facts: Between inferior and superior articular process facets; synovial, prone to arthritis
Facetogenic pain: classically worse with extension, relieved by flexion; cervical facets commonly cause headache
spine.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 19, 36

cervical_vertebrae.name: Cervical vertebrae
facts: Small bodies, large vertebral foramen, transverse foramina, bifid spinous process
C7 prominens is a palpable back landmark
cervical_vertebrae.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 9, 20

thoracic_vertebrae.name: Thoracic vertebrae
facts: Small vertebral foramen, long transverse and spinous processes, costal facets articulating with ribs
thoracic_vertebrae.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 20

lumbar_vertebrae.name: Lumbar vertebrae
facts: Large bodies, large vertebral foramen, no costal facets
lumbar_vertebrae.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 20

atlas.name: Atlas (C1)
facts: Lateral masses, anterior and posterior arches; labelled the 'yes' vertebra
atlas.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 21

axis.name: Axis (C2)
facts: Has the dens; labelled the 'no' vertebra
axis.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 21

sacrum.name: Sacrum
facts: Five fused vertebrae; palpable back structure
sacrum.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 9, 16

coccyx.name: Coccyx
facts: Four fused vertebrae
coccyx.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 16

hip_bone.name: Iliac crest
facts: Palpable back structure
hip_bone.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 9

hip_bone.name: Iliac crest
facts: Level of L4 in surface anatomy.
hip_bone.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 6

hip_bone.name: ASIS (anterior superior iliac spine)
facts: Origin of tensor fascia latae and sartorius.
hip_bone.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 8, 33

hip_bone.name: AIIS (anterior inferior iliac spine)
facts: Origin of rectus femoris.
hip_bone.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 34

hip_bone.name: Ischial tuberosity
facts: Origin of the hamstrings (biceps femoris long head, semimembranosus, semitendinosus).
Surface landmark of the gluteal region.
hip_bone.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 6, 22, 23

hip_bone.name: Greater sciatic foramen
facts: Piriformis exits the pelvis through it.
hip_bone.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 4, 11

ribs.name: Ribs 6-12
facts: Palpable back structures
ribs.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 9

clavicle.name: Clavicle
facts: Pectoral girdle bone with sternal and acromial ends
Forms the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints
clavicle.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 3

scapula.name: Scapula
facts: Landmarks: acromion, coracoid process, glenoid fossa, superior and inferior angles
Fossae: subscapular (anterior), supraspinous and infraspinous (posterior)
Scapulothoracic joint is one of the four pectoral girdle joints
scapula.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 4, 9

scapula.name: Acromion
facts: Scapular landmark; meets the clavicle at the acromioclavicular (AC) joint
scapula.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 4, 11

scapula.name: Coracoid process
facts: Scapular landmark; coracoclavicular ligament joins it to the clavicle
scapula.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 4, 11

scapula.name: Glenoid fossa
facts: Socket of the glenohumeral joint, lined by hyaline cartilage and deepened by the labrum
scapula.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 4, 14

scapula.name: Supraglenoid tubercle
facts: Origin of the long head of biceps brachii, together with the superior glenoid labrum

scapula.name: Infraglenoid tubercle
facts: Origin of the long head of triceps

humerus.name: Humerus (proximal)
facts: Head, greater and lesser tubercles, intertubercular groove, radial (spiral) groove
Head articulates with the glenoid fossa at the glenohumeral joint
humerus.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 5

humerus.name: Humerus (distal)
facts: Trochlea, capitulum, medial and lateral epicondyles, coronoid and olecranon fossae
humerus.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 6

humerus.name: Humerus
facts: Distal humerus forms the elbow joint with the ulna (humeroulnar) and radius (humeroradial).
humerus.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 2, 3

humerus.name: Trochlea
facts: Distal humerus landmark at the elbow.
humerus.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 2

humerus.name: Capitulum
facts: Distal humerus landmark at the elbow.
humerus.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 2

humerus.name: Coronoid fossa
facts: Distal humerus landmark at the elbow.
humerus.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 2

humerus.name: Medial epicondyle
facts: Common origin of anterior compartment (flexor-pronator) muscles.
Ulnar nerve passes posterior to it (the 'funny bone').
Medial epicondylosis (golfer's elbow) is tendinopathy at the common flexor origin here.
humerus.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 4, 42

humerus.name: Lateral epicondyle
facts: Common origin of posterior compartment (extensor-supinator) muscles.
Lateral epicondylosis (tennis elbow): pain just distal to it.
humerus.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 17, 40

humerus.name: Elbow joint
facts: Synovial hinge joint with two articulations: humeroradial and humeroulnar.
humerus.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 3

ulna.name: Olecranon
facts: Ulnar landmark at the elbow; fits the olecranon fossa of the humerus
ulna.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 6

ulna.name: Coronoid process (ulna)
facts: Ulnar landmark labelled at the elbow
ulna.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 6

ulna.name: Coronoid process
facts: Proximal ulna landmark at the elbow.
ulna.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 2

ulna.name: Olecranon
facts: Covered by the subcutaneous olecranon bursa, the most common superficial bursitis.
ulna.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 4, 28

ulna.name: Ulnar head
facts: Distal ulna landmark at the wrist.
ulna.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 8

ulna.name: Ulnar styloid process
facts: Distal ulna landmark at the wrist.
ulna.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 8

radius.name: Radial head
facts: Radial landmark labelled at the elbow
radius.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 6

radius.name: Radial tuberosity
facts: Radial landmark labelled at the elbow
radius.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 6

radius.name: Radial head
facts: Articulates with the radial notch of the ulna at the proximal radioulnar joint.
Subluxes in young children after traction on the arm (nursemaid's elbow).
radius.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 2, 7, 22

radius.name: Radial tuberosity
facts: Proximal radius landmark at the elbow.
radius.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 2

radius.name: Radial styloid process
facts: Distal radius landmark at the wrist.
radius.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 8

radius.name: Radioulnar joints
facts: Proximal and distal are synovial pivot joints; intermediate is a syndesmosis (interosseous membrane).
Proximal joint lies within the elbow joint capsule; anular ligament allows rotation.
Allow supination and pronation.
radius.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 5, 6, 7

radius.name: Distal radius
facts: Fracture: very common, FOOSH (fall on outstretched hand); poor function if anatomy not restored.
Assess three parameters: crooked/bent (articular angle), length (ulnar variance), joint surface.
>1 mm articular step associated with post-traumatic arthrosis; shortening causes ulnar impaction syndrome.

carpals.name: Carpal bones
facts: Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.
Mnemonic: Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle.
carpals.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 8

carpals.name: Trapezium
facts: Carpal bone lying in the anatomical snuff box with the scaphoid.
carpals.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 26

carpals.name: Hook of hamate
facts: Hamate landmark labelled on the wrist osteology slide.
carpals.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 8

carpals.name: Carpal bones
facts: Form the floor of the carpal tunnel.
With an overlying ligament form the ulnar (Guyon's) canal.

scaphoid.name: Scaphoid
facts: Carpal bone lying in the anatomical snuff box with the trapezium.
scaphoid.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 26

scaphoid.name: Scaphoid
facts: Most common carpal bone fracture, young people; retrograde blood flow risks nonunion and osteonecrosis.
If X-rays normal but suspicious: treat as fractured, get CT or MRI.
Undisplaced/distal: cast until union; displaced/proximal: surgery.

metacarpals.name: Metacarpals
facts: Five metacarpals; carpometacarpal (CMC) joints proximally, metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints distally.
metacarpals.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 9

metacarpals.name: Hand joints (CMC, MCP, IP)
facts: IP joints hinge; MCP joints condyloid; CMC plane in digits 2-5, saddle in digit 1 (allows opposition).
All supported by joint capsule and extensive ligamentous support.

phalanges_hand.name: Phalanges
facts: Proximal, middle and distal phalanges joined at interphalangeal (IP) joints.
Digits numbered 1-5: thumb, index, long, ring, small.
phalanges_hand.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 9, 10

femur.name: Greater trochanter
facts: Insertion of gluteus medius and minimus; surface landmark.
femur.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 6, 9

femur.name: Femoral neck
facts: Hip fracture means proximal femur fracture: femoral neck (subcapital), intertrochanteric, subtrochanteric.
Displaced neck fractures need arthroplasty (hemi or total) to preserve femoral head blood supply.
Intertrochanteric and subtrochanteric fractures: intramedullary nail.
femur.src: Clinical Approach to the Hip, slide 18, 27, 31, 33

femur.name: Femur
facts: Knee joint has 3 articulations
femur.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 4

femur.name: Lateral femoral condyle
facts: Origin of popliteus and lateral head of gastrocnemius
femur.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 4

femur.name: Medial femoral condyle
facts: Origin of medial head of gastrocnemius
femur.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 4

femur.name: Intercondylar fossa (notch)
facts: Posterior femur between the condyles
femur.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 6

femur.name: Patellar surface
facts: Femoral surface forming the patellofemoral joint
femur.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 5

tibia.name: Tibial tuberosity
facts: Quadriceps insert here via the quadriceps tendon.
tibia.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 34

tibia.name: Pes anserinus
facts: Insertion of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus (SGT) on the medial tibia.
tibia.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 23, 33, 42

tibia.name: Tibia
facts: Origin of soleus with the fibula
tibia.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 4

tibia.name: Lateral tibial condyle
facts: Proximal tibia, lateral side of the knee joint
tibia.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 4

tibia.name: Medial tibial condyle
facts: Proximal tibia, medial side of the knee joint
tibia.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 4

tibia.name: Tibial tuberosity
facts: Attachment of the patellar tendon; may avulse in a PCL (posterior cruciate ligament) dashboard injury
tibia.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 4, 13

tibia.name: Intercondylar eminence
facts: Proximal tibia between the tibial condyles
tibia.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 4

tibia.name: Medial malleolus
facts: Tip/posterior edge tenderness: Ottawa ankle x-ray criterion
Posterior tibial pulse felt between it and calcaneal tendon
tibia.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 28, 41

fibula.name: Head of fibula
facts: Insertion of biceps femoris.
fibula.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 22

fibula.name: Fibula
facts: Origin of soleus with the tibia

fibula.name: Head of fibula
facts: Proximal fibula, lateral to the knee

fibula.name: Lateral malleolus
facts: Tip/posterior edge tenderness: Ottawa ankle x-ray criterion
Fractured with medial malleolus in a bimalleolar fracture, usually forceful eversion
fibula.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 28, 31

patella.name: Patella
facts: Tends to subluxate laterally during knee extension
Countered by pull of vastus medialis and an extra buttress of bone on the lateral patellar surface
patella.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 2, slide 4, 5

talus.name: Talus
facts: Trochlea articulates with tibia and fibula at the talocrural joint; wider anteriorly, so most congruent in dorsiflexion
Inferior surface forms the subtalar joint with calcaneus, where most inversion/eversion occurs
talus.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 16, 19

calcaneus.name: Calcaneus
facts: Calcaneal tendon inserts on its posterior surface
Plantar fasciitis pain at the anteromedial calcaneus

calcaneus.name: Calcaneal tuberosity
facts: Posterior calcaneus

calcaneus.name: Sustentaculum tali
facts: Flexor hallucis longus tendon runs beneath it

navicular.name: Navicular
facts: Tenderness is an Ottawa foot x-ray criterion
navicular.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 28

cuboid.name: Cuboid
facts: Part of the transverse arch
cuboid.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 22

cuneiforms.name: Cuneiforms
facts: Part of the transverse arch
cuneiforms.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 22

metatarsals.name: Tuberosity of 5th metatarsal
facts: Fibularis brevis inserts at the base of the 5th metatarsal
Base of 5th metatarsal tenderness is an Ottawa foot x-ray criterion

metatarsals.name: Heads of metatarsals
facts: Bear half of body weight; the calcaneus bears the other half
metatarsals.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 23

Back.title: Red flags in back and neck pain
Back.text: Neurologic, inflammatory, neoplastic, infectious, fracture and vascular red flags suggest a sinister cause; e.g. saddle anaesthesia, night pain, weight loss, fever, IV drug use, osteoporosis.
Back.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 6

Back.title: Mechanical back pain
Back.text: Axial pain worse with movement and relieved by rest, midline or peri-midline, with no red flags; often degenerative and 'tweaked' by an acute event.
Back.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 14

Back.title: Who to image
Back.text: No red flags and symptoms under 6 weeks: no imaging. X-ray only for red flags or persistent pain despite treatment; CT only if MRI cannot be done.
Back.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 58

Back.title: Discogenic pain
Back.text: Internal disc disruption may cause 20-40% of back pain: axial-predominant, mechanical, worse with forward flexion. Managed conservatively with therapy, exercise, NSAIDs or acetaminophen.
Back.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 30

Back.title: Disc herniation
Back.text: Causes both discogenic pain and nerve compression; acute herniation in younger people after lifting, worse with coughing or sneezing; lumbar discs herniate posterolaterally toward nerve roots.
Back.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 31

Back.title: Facetogenic pain
Back.text: Facet joint arthritis: localized axial pain, headache in cervical spine, rarely past the knee in lumbar spine; worse with extension, relieved by flexion. Flexion-based therapy, NSAIDs, injections.
Back.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 38

Back.title: Spondylosis and stenosis
Back.text: Degenerative disc disease plus facet arthropathy; progression to subluxation, osteophytes, ligament hypertrophy and spondylolisthesis can narrow neural foramina (lateral stenosis) or the central canal.
Back.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 62

Back.title: Muscle problems
Back.text: Acute strain/spasm, repetitive strain and myofascial trigger points have no diagnostic test; manage conservatively with reassurance, relative rest, ice/heat, short NSAIDs and physiotherapy.
Back.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 53

Back.title: Whiplash associated disorder
Back.text: Acceleration/deceleration neck injury, most often muscle strain; most improve conservatively: keep moving, avoid C-collars, modest physiotherapy. X-ray if fracture concern, MRI if neurological signs.
Back.src: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back Pain, slide 55

Shoulder.title: Acromioclavicular (AC) joint problems
Shoulder.text: Acute injury causes AC separation (grades I-V, increasing displacement); gradual onset suggests osteoarthritis. Grades I-III: education, sling, ice, early exercise; IV-V: surgery.
Shoulder.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 25

Shoulder.title: Shoulder arthritis
Shoulder.text: Noninflammatory: reduced active and passive motion, cuff strength intact, asymmetric joint space, osteophytes. Inflammatory: passive > active motion, weak cuff, symmetric joint space, erosions, osteopenia.
Shoulder.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 35

Shoulder.title: Shoulder replacement
Shoulder.text: Anatomic or reverse arthroplasty: 85% good or excellent, 90% survive 10 years; complications include infection, loosening, instability, fracture.
Shoulder.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 43

Shoulder.title: Shoulder instability
Shoulder.text: Traumatic: unidirectional, mostly anterior, 'torn loose', surgery (labral repair) often for young recurrent dislocators. Atraumatic (AMBRI): multidirectional, 'born loose', physiotherapy first, inferior capsular shift.
Shoulder.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 55

Shoulder.title: Glenoid labrum
Shoulder.text: Increases surface area and depth of the glenoid and acts as a bumper; ligaments, labrum, bones, rotator cuff/muscle forces and nerves all contribute to stability.
Shoulder.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 51

Shoulder.title: Adhesive capsulitis
Shoulder.text: Spontaneous global loss of active AND passive motion with normal X-rays; 2% of adults, 20% of diabetics, onset 40s-50s; freezing, frozen, thawing stages; usually self-limited.
Shoulder.src: Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 72

Shoulder.title: Rotator cuff disease
Shoulder.text: Most common shoulder disorder, onset 40s, progressive; intrinsic (vascularity, tendon degeneration) or extrinsic (acromion morphology). Painful arc, Neer and Hawkins impingement signs; staged I-III to arthropathy.

Shoulder.title: Rotator cuff treatment
Shoulder.text: Mostly nonsurgical: education, NSAIDs, physiotherapy, injections. Stage I: physio or subacromial decompression; Stage II: consider repair; Stage III (full thickness): repair.

Shoulder.title: Winged scapula
Shoulder.text: Long thoracic nerve lesion: serratus anterior cannot hold the medial border of the scapula against the thoracic wall when pushing with the upper limb.

Shoulder.title: Brachial plexus roots and branches
Shoulder.text: Ventral rami C5-T1: roots, trunks, divisions, cords, terminal branches. Axillary C5-6, musculocutaneous C5-7, radial and median C5-T1, ulnar C8-T1.

Arm.title: Arm compartments
Arm.text: Anterior compartment flexes shoulder and elbow and supinates (musculocutaneous nerve); posterior compartment extends shoulder and elbow (radial nerve).

Arm.title: Proximal biceps tendinopathy
Arm.text: Common anterior shoulder pain; tender in intertubercular groove, worse with flexion when supinated. Differential: rotator cuff, bursitis, SLAP tear, arthritis, radiculopathy. Ultrasound helps; physiotherapy is mainstay.

Arm.title: C8 radiculopathy is not shoulder pain
Arm.text: Higher cervical radiculopathy (C4 or C5) may cause shoulder complaints, but C8 radiculopathy typically gives pain or paraesthesiae in the hand.

Arm.title: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
Arm.text: The radial nerve (C5-T1) runs in the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus, a site at risk of injury; it supplies the posterior compartment.
Arm.src: Neurovascular Supply to the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 12

Arm.title: Brachial artery and humeral fractures
Arm.text: The brachial artery is used to measure blood pressure and is susceptible to humeral shaft fractures.
Arm.src: Neurovascular Supply to the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 5

Arm.title: Bicipital reflex
Arm.text: The bicipital myotatic reflex tests the integrity of C5 and C6.
Arm.src: Neurovascular Supply to the Proximal Upper Extremity, slide 11

Arm.title: Distal biceps rupture
Arm.text: Rare but consequential: anterior elbow pain, poor supination and weak flexion after a pop; refer to orthopedics urgently. Proximal ruptures are commoner and usually managed non-operatively.
Arm.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 43

Forearm.title: Lateral epicondylosis (tennis elbow)
Forearm.text: Common (1-3%/year), 30s-40s, mostly occupational. Mainly extensor carpi radialis brevis tendinopathy. Pain just distal to lateral epicondyle, worse gripping and supinating, with resisted middle-finger/wrist extension, and passive stretch.
Forearm.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 40

Forearm.title: Medial epicondylosis (golfer's elbow)
Forearm.text: Tendinopathy at the common flexor origin. Pain at the origin, with resisted wrist flexion and pronation, and with passive stretch.
Forearm.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 42

Forearm.title: Tendinitis vs tendinosis
Forearm.text: Tendinitis is true inflammation (rheumatologic, acute overload, infection); treat inflammation, faster recovery. Tendinosis is collagen degeneration from chronic overuse; more common, slow (100+ days) recovery.
Forearm.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 39

Forearm.title: Managing tendinopathy
Forearm.text: Educate, modify the offending activity, ice/RICE, counterforce strap for tennis elbow, PT eccentric strengthening twice daily for 12 weeks; topical anti-inflammatories; surgical referral if refractory.
Forearm.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 44

Forearm.title: Elbow osteoarthritis
Forearm.text: Gradual achy pain, stiffness, loss of range of motion, locking. X-ray: joint-space loss, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis/cysts. PT/OT, topical anti-inflammatories, acetaminophen, NSAIDs, steroid injection; arthroplasty if end stage.
Forearm.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 18

Forearm.title: Elbow dislocation
Forearm.text: Usually fall onto outstretched hand (FOOSH); posterior is most common. Red flag: capsule and ligament rupture, ulnar nerve at risk, compartment syndrome. Closed reduction and splint at 90 degrees, or open reduction internal fixation.
Forearm.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 21

Forearm.title: Radial head subluxation (nursemaid's elbow)
Forearm.text: Children under 5, girls and left arm more often. Pain after traction on the arm; holds arm flexed and refuses to use it. Closed reduction by pronation and extension; image only to exclude fracture.
Forearm.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 22

Forearm.title: Ulnar collateral ligament injury
Forearm.text: Repetitive overuse (baseball pitchers); may pop at medial elbow. Medial tenderness, no end point on valgus stress. PT, orthoses; reconstruction (Tommy John surgery) only if needed for function.
Forearm.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 23

Forearm.title: Olecranon bursitis
Forearm.text: Most common superficial bursitis, from a fall on the elbow or repeated leaning. Red, hot, systemically unwell suggests septic bursitis: aspirate and give antibiotics. Otherwise pad, ice, NSAIDs.
Forearm.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 28

Forearm.title: Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow (cubital tunnel)
Forearm.text: From a hit to the funny bone, leaning, or sleeping flexed. Medial elbow pain, numbness into ring and small fingers, positive Tinel sign; small hand muscles weaken first. EMG/NCS; avoid pressure and hyperflexion.
Forearm.src: Neurovascular Supply to the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 23

Forearm.title: Pronator syndrome
Forearm.text: Median nerve entrapment where it passes between the two heads of pronator teres.
Forearm.src: Neurovascular Supply to the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 10

Forearm.title: Cubital fossa
Forearm.text: Bounded by brachioradialis, pronator teres and the epicondyle line; holds biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve (TAN), with median cubital vein superficially. Pictured uses: IV access, blood pressure, venipuncture.
Forearm.src: Neurovascular Supply to the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 6

Forearm.title: Elbow pain by location
Forearm.text: Anterior: arthritis, distal biceps. Medial: medial epicondylosis, ulnar neuritis, UCL tear. Lateral: lateral epicondylosis. Posterior: olecranon bursitis, arthritis, triceps tendinopathy. Fracture anywhere.
Forearm.src: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity and the Elbow, slide 15

Hand.title: Ganglion (synovial) cyst
Hand.text: Cyst of clear mucinous fluid, usually on the dorsum of the wrist, communicating with synovial sheaths ('Bible bump'). Leave alone, drain or excise.
Hand.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 30

Hand.title: Mallet finger
Hand.text: Cannot extend the DIP joint after the extensor tendon partly tears from the base of the distal phalanx. RICE and splinting; complete avulsion fracture needs surgical pinning.
Hand.src: Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 31

Hand.title: Carpal tunnel syndrome
Hand.text: Median nerve compression where it passes deep to the flexor retinaculum.
Hand.src: Neurovascular Supply to the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 10

Hand.title: Ulnar (Guyon's) canal
Hand.text: Site at the wrist where the ulnar nerve is at risk of injury; less common than compression at the elbow.
Hand.src: Neurovascular Supply to the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 12

Hand.title: Superficial radial nerve in the snuff box
Hand.text: The superficial (dorsal sensory) branch of the radial nerve, sensory to the dorsum of the hand lateral to the 4th digit, is at risk in the anatomical snuff box.
Hand.src: Neurovascular Supply to the Distal Upper Extremity, slide 16

Hand.title: Distal radius fracture treatment
Hand.text: Treatment depends on age/activity and displacement: adequate analgesia, closed reduction (traction, increase deformity, correct) and casting with 3-point mold; surgical reduction if inadequate; then rehabilitation.

Hand.title: Scaphoid fracture complications
Hand.text: Tenuous retrograde blood supply: delayed diagnosis leads to nonunion, osteonecrosis and late arthrosis. Be suspicious: treat as fractured if X-ray normal.

Hand.title: Carpal tunnel syndrome
Hand.text: Median nerve compression at the wrist; night numbness/tingling in median territory, worse with flexed/extended wrist, possible APB weakness, Tinel/Phalen signs; median forearm muscles normal.

Hand.title: Carpal tunnel causes
Hand.text: Extrinsic: fracture, flexor tenosynovitis, ganglia, inflammation, pregnancy, acromegaly. Intrinsic: diabetes, amyloidosis, alcohol. Very commonly idiopathic.

Hand.title: Carpal tunnel: differential and management
Hand.text: Main differential C6 radiculopathy; EMG/NCS (electromyography/nerve conduction) helps. Manage with education, overnight wrist orthosis, corticosteroid injection, carpal tunnel release.

Hand.title: Ulnar canal (Guyon's) syndrome
Hand.text: Ulnar nerve compression in Guyon's canal (fracture, ganglia, inflammation, handlebar neuropathy): hypoesthesia of medial 1½ digits, intrinsic hand weakness. Differential C8 radiculopathy, ulnar nerve at elbow.

Hand.title: Ulnar neuropathy management
Hand.text: Education on hand position and pressure; relieve pressure (specialized gloves, change handlebars); Guyon's release.

Hip & thigh.title: Sciatic nerve injury
Hip & thigh.text: Sciatic nerve (L4-S3; tibial plus common peroneal) injury gives buttock pain or numbness radiating down the leg; causes: herniated disc, hip surgery, piriformis syndrome, intragluteal injection.
Hip & thigh.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 16

Hip & thigh.title: Limp after hip replacement (knowledge check)
Hip & thigh.text: Pelvis drops on the side of the swinging leg after total hip replacement; slide asks which muscle, side and nerve (answer not on slide).
Hip & thigh.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 12

Hip & thigh.title: Hamstring avulsion (knowledge check)
Hip & thigh.text: Hurdler feels a pop in posterior thigh, later extensive posterior thigh bleeding; X-ray shows an avulsion fracture.
Hip & thigh.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 25

Hip & thigh.title: Groin pull
Hip & thigh.text: Active contraction and passive stretch of medial compartment muscles; bruising and pain; conservative treatment with RICE and NSAIDs.
Hip & thigh.src: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region and Thigh, slide 43

Hip & thigh.title: Hip fracture presentation
Hip & thigh.text: Sudden groin/lateral thigh pain after a fall; shortened, externally rotated, abducted limb; cannot weight bear. High suspicion in elderly. AP pelvis/hip X-ray; CT if negative but suspicious.
Hip & thigh.src: Clinical Approach to the Hip, slide 16

Hip & thigh.title: Hip fracture work-up
Hip & thigh.text: Check stability (ABCs), pelvic fracture, distal pulses and sciatic nerve; ask why they fell (CBC, electrolytes, troponin, ECG, chest X-ray) and why they fractured (pathologic, osteoporosis).
Hip & thigh.src: Clinical Approach to the Hip, slide 24

Hip & thigh.title: Hip fracture management
Hip & thigh.text: Surgical fixation within 24-48 hours is standard; neck fractures: screws or arthroplasty; inter/subtrochanteric: intramedullary nail. Prevent VTE (LMWH 14-30 days), pneumonia, delirium; mobilize early.
Hip & thigh.src: Clinical Approach to the Hip, slide 35

Leg.title: ACL injury
Leg.text: Non-contact cutting/pivoting on deceleration; female 4.5:1. 'Pop', immediate hemarthrosis, giving way. Lachman, anterior drawer, pivot shift; MRI if unclear; reconstruction; return to play 9-12 months.
Leg.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 17

Leg.title: PCL injury
Leg.text: Direct blow to anterior tibia with knee flexed (dashboard) or hyperextension; poorly defined pain, minimal swelling. Posterior drawer, sag sign, reverse Lachman; physiotherapy usually sufficient.
Leg.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 19

Leg.title: MCL and LCL injuries
Leg.text: MCL: very common, valgus collision, minimal swelling, early range of motion and bracing. LCL: uncommon alone, high-energy varus, associated with PCL injury.
Leg.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 21

Leg.title: Meniscal injuries
Leg.text: Rotation with foot planted; joint line pain, delayed swelling, locking/catching. McMurray and Thessaly tests; MRI if failing conservative care. Repair vs resection depends on zone and age.
Leg.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 36

Leg.title: Unhappy triad
Leg.text: Forced valgus tears the MCL, then a bucket-handle tear of the attached medial meniscus, then abduction, external rotation and slight flexion tear the ACL.
Leg.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 39

Leg.title: Screw-home mechanism
Leg.text: Femur rotates medially on tibia in the last 15-20 degrees of extension, tightening the ligaments; popliteus laterally rotates the femur 5 degrees to unlock.
Leg.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 1, slide 29

Leg.title: Patellofemoral pain syndrome
Leg.text: Anterior knee ache after loading, prolonged sitting, stairs; no swelling. Females, adolescents, increased Q-angle. Clinical diagnosis; physiotherapy balancing vastus lateralis and vastus medialis.
Leg.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 2, slide 8

Leg.title: Knee bursitis
Leg.text: Prepatellar, infrapatellar, suprapatellar bursae; friction irritation; mild swelling and tenderness over the bursa. PRICE, NSAIDs. Don't confuse with septic bursitis.
Leg.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 2, slide 12

Leg.title: Popliteal (Baker's) cyst
Leg.text: Synovial extension through posterior capsule defects into the popliteal fossa. Ultrasound confirms. Differential: popliteal artery aneurysm, DVT (deep vein thrombosis), tumour, meniscal cyst. Conservative 6 weeks.
Leg.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 2, slide 13

Leg.title: IT band friction syndrome
Leg.text: Friction between ITB and lateral epicondyle below 30 degrees of flexion; running, especially downhill. Aching lateral knee. PRICE, stretch ITB.
Leg.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 2, slide 14

Leg.title: Traumatic knee swelling timing
Leg.text: Swelling under 6 hours: ACL tear, fracture, patellar dislocation, large chondral injury. Over 6 hours: OA flare, meniscal, PCL, high-grade MCL.
Leg.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 2, slide 25

Leg.title: Knee injections
Leg.text: Corticosteroid: rapid, cheap, short-acting. Hyaluronic acid: over 26 weeks relief, expensive. PRP: no clinically significant benefit on Cochrane review. Stem cells: unproven, regulated as drugs.
Leg.src: Clinical Approach to the Knee, part 2, slide 16

Leg.title: Four compartments of the leg
Leg.text: Anterior (dorsiflexion, deep fibular nerve), lateral (eversion, superficial fibular nerve), superficial posterior (plantarflexion, tibial nerve), deep posterior (tibial nerve, under flexor retinaculum).

Leg.title: Venous return and varicose veins
Leg.text: Valves, arteriovenous and musculovenous pumps return blood. Dilated great saphenous vein with incompetent valves gives varicose veins; laser treatment scars the vein closed.

Foot.title: Tarsal tunnel
Foot.text: Anterior to posterior: Tibialis posterior, flexor Digitorum longus, posterior tibial Artery and Vein, tibial Nerve, flexor Hallucis longus.

Foot.title: Achilles tendinopathy and rupture
Foot.text: Runners after training increase; posterior heel pain, worse with passive dorsiflexion. Eccentric strengthening. Rupture in active 30-40s; surgery vs casting, surgery risks sural nerve injury.
Foot.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 9

Foot.title: Plantar fasciitis
Foot.text: Chronic insertional inflammation; anteromedial calcaneal pain on first morning steps, 40-60 years, F>M; tight Achilles. Heel pad, arch support, stretching, night splints.
Foot.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 13

Foot.title: Lateral ankle sprain
Foot.text: Up to 85% of sprains; inversion and plantarflexion. ATFL > CFL > PTFL. Anterior drawer test of ATFL. Early mobilization, strengthening, proprioception.
Foot.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 26

Foot.title: Ottawa foot and ankle rules
Foot.text: X-ray if malleolar/midfoot pain plus bone tenderness at either malleolus posterior edge/tip, base of 5th metatarsal, or navicular, or inability to bear weight.
Foot.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 28

Foot.title: Ankle fractures
Foot.text: Unimalleolar may be non-operative; bimalleolar (forceful eversion) and trimalleolar need surgery. Maisonneuve: forceful external rotation, interosseous ligament disruption, usually surgical.
Foot.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 31

Foot.title: Tibialis posterior dysfunction and pes planus
Foot.text: Tendon hypovascular distal to medial malleolus; medial ankle pain, flexible then rigid flat foot, 'too many toes' sign. Strengthening, orthoses.
Foot.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 34

Foot.title: Bunions (hallux valgus)
Foot.text: Footwear and metatarsus varus; medial first MTP (metatarsophalangeal) pain; poor toe-off. Wider toe box; surgical realignment.
Foot.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 46

Foot.title: Morton's neuroma
Foot.text: Perineural fibrosis of common digital nerve, usually between 3rd and 4th metatarsals; burning dysesthesia, worse in narrow high heels; squeeze test.
Foot.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 48

Foot.title: Diabetic foot
Foot.text: Microvascular disease and neuropathy cause insensate foot, intrinsic atrophy, Charcot joint, ulcers (15% of diabetics). Monofilament test, proper footwear, daily foot checks.
Foot.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 50

Foot.title: Arterial pulses of the foot
Foot.text: Absent dorsalis pedis pulse suggests arterial disease; five P's of occlusion. Posterior tibial pulse between medial malleolus and calcaneal tendon, compare sides.
Foot.src: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, slide 39
